en: Agreement or harmony; a formal treaty; to give or grant
hook: ACCORD: hearts (cor) in agreement.
story: Accord. Two families near Comilla had quarrelled for years over a narrow strip of land between their fields. Finally, the elders brought them together under the banyan tree. After hours of talk, both sides agreed to share the strip as a footpath. They had reached an accord: an agreement, a state of harmony. An accord can also be a formal treaty, like a peace accord. As a verb, to accord means to give or grant, as in according someone respect. Synonyms: agreement, pact.

gre.s: After decades of hostility, the two neighboring states finally reached a historic ____ on sharing the river's waters, though skeptics doubted it would survive the next drought.
gre.clue: though skeptics doubted it would survive the next drought

example: Under the new accord, the two universities will let their students take courses at either campus without paying extra fees.

en: Harmful or unfavorable
hook: ADVERSE: like an ADVERSARY, working against you.
story: Adverse. The fishermen of Kuakata had planned to go out to sea on Monday, but the weather office reported adverse conditions: strong winds, rough waves, and a depression forming in the Bay of Bengal. Every boat stayed on the shore. Adverse means harmful or unfavourable. Medicines can have adverse effects. Careful: do not confuse adverse with averse, which means unwilling, as in averse to risk. Conditions are adverse; people are averse. Synonyms: unfavourable, harmful, hostile.

gre.s: The drug trial was halted early because several participants suffered ____ reactions, including severe rashes and dangerously high fevers.
gre.clue: including severe rashes and dangerously high fevers

example: Doctors warned that staying up past midnight before every exam can have adverse effects on both memory and mood.

en: Based on random choice or personal whim rather than reason
hook: ARBITRARY: like an ARBITER who decides by flipping a coin.
story: Arbitrary. The new hostel warden announced his rules. No showers after nine on Tuesdays. No blue shirts on Fridays. Guests allowed only on days ending in Y, except Wednesday. When students asked why, he said, "Because I said so." The rules were arbitrary: based on whim or chance rather than reason. An arbitrary decision feels unfair because nothing justifies it. Imagine a referee who decides every call by flipping a coin.

gre.s: Employees resented the new promotion policy, which seemed entirely ____, rewarding some workers and passing over others for no discernible reason.
gre.clue: for no discernible reason

example: The border between the two provinces looks arbitrary on the map, a straight line drawn by colonial officials who never visited the region.

en: To regard something as caused by; a quality or feature
hook: ATTRIBUTE: give TRIBUTE (credit) to the cause.
story: Attribute. One summer, Mahin's mango tree suddenly produced twice as much fruit as usual. His father attributed it to the new fertiliser; his mother attributed it to her daily prayers; the neighbour attributed it to pure luck. To attribute is to regard something as caused by a particular source. As a noun, stressed on the first syllable, an attribute is a quality or feature: patience is a fine attribute in a teacher. Synonyms: ascribe, credit, assign.

gre.s: Although the coach was quick to ____ the team's victory to his new training regimen, most observers credited the opposing goalkeeper's uncharacteristic blunders.
gre.clue: most observers credited the opposing goalkeeper's uncharacteristic blunders

example: Doctors attribute this year's sharp rise in dengue cases to an unusually long and wet monsoon season.

en: Serving as an extra or backup source of help
hook: AUXILIARY: AUX cable, extra support.
story: Auxiliary. During a power cut at a Dhaka hospital, the lights in the operating theatre flickered off for two seconds, then came back on as the auxiliary generator started humming. The surgeons never even paused. An auxiliary generator provides additional help or support when the main system fails. In grammar, auxiliary verbs like have and will help the main verb. The word comes from the Latin auxilium, meaning help. Synonyms: supplementary, backup, ancillary.

gre.s: Although the main pump handles routine cooling, engineers installed ____ pumps that switch on automatically whenever demand exceeds its capacity.
gre.clue: whenever demand exceeds its capacity

example: When the main ferry broke down, the company sent two auxiliary boats so that passengers would not miss the Eid rush home.

en: Having enough skill or knowledge to do something successfully
hook: COMPETENT: able to COMPETE.
story: Competent. Tanvir is not the most brilliant programmer in his office. He does not invent clever tricks or win hackathons. But every task he takes on gets done correctly, on time, and without bugs. His manager trusts him with anything. He is competent: having enough skill or knowledge to do something successfully. A competent doctor may not be famous, but you can trust her with your life. Competence is quiet reliability.

gre.s: Although not brilliant, the new manager proved thoroughly ____, handling every crisis calmly and efficiently.
gre.clue: handling every crisis calmly and efficiently

example: Nasrin is a competent driver, but she still asks her brother to take the wheel on the busy Dhaka-Chattogram highway.

en: Believable enough to be trusted or taken seriously
hook: CREDIBLE: has CREDIT, so you can believe it.
story: Credible. Two stories appeared on Imran's phone on the same morning. The first, from a major newspaper, quoted named officials, showed signed documents, and included dated photographs. The second, forwarded by an unknown number, claimed that eating garlic cures every disease, with no source at all. Only the first was credible: believable and trustworthy. Credible shares a root with credit, meaning belief. Before sharing information online, ask whether its source is credible.

gre.s: The jury found the witness's account ____, since it matched the physical evidence in every detail.
gre.clue: it matched the physical evidence in every detail

example: For a threat of punishment to work, a parent must make it credible, so empty warnings soon lose their effect.

en: To restrain or keep in check
hook: CURB: the street CURB keeps cars from going too far.
story: Curb. Joya's monthly allowance kept disappearing on food delivery apps. By the twentieth of every month, she was borrowing money from her roommate. So she made a rule: no deliveries on weekdays, and only one treat on Friday. She was curbing her spending: restraining it and keeping it in check. A curb is also the raised edge of a road that keeps cars off the footpath, and a curb on a horse's bridle holds it back. Synonyms: restrain, check, rein in.

gre.s: Hoping to ____ the spread of the disease, health officials closed schools and banned large gatherings for a month, despite protests from businesses.
gre.clue: closed schools and banned large gatherings

example: The central bank raised interest rates to curb inflation, which had pushed the price of onions to a record high.

en: Done consciously and intentionally (adj.); to think carefully before deciding (verb)
hook: DELIBERATE: done with LIBERTY of choice, on purpose.
story: Deliberate. With five minutes left and his team winning by one goal, the defender grabbed the opposing striker's shirt and pulled him to the ground. It was no accident. It was a deliberate foul to stop a certain goal. The referees then deliberated for ten minutes before showing a red card. As an adjective, deliberate means intentional, or slow and careful. As a verb, to deliberate means to think carefully before deciding.

gre.s: Investigators concluded that the fire was not an accident but a ____ act, pointing to traces of fuel poured near every exit.
gre.clue: pointing to traces of fuel poured near every exit

example: The professor's long pause before answering was deliberate, a way of making the students think harder about their own question.

en: To overshadow; to surpass or make less important
hook: ECLIPSE: like the moon blocking out the sun.
story: Eclipse. Nadia was the family star: top of her class, debate champion, president of every club. Then her younger sister Priya started winning international math olympiads. Newspapers interviewed her. The prime minister shook her hand. At every family gathering, relatives only talked about Priya. Her fame had eclipsed Nadia's: overshadowed it, made it seem less important, like the moon blocking the sun. A new world record can eclipse an old one.

gre.s: Although the novelist was celebrated in her lifetime, her reputation came to ____ that of her more famous brother only after both had died.
gre.clue: her more famous brother

example: The huge success of her second album soon eclipsed her debut, which few listeners now remember.

en: Originating from a distant foreign country; strikingly unusual
hook: EXOTIC: EXternal, from the outside world.
story: Exotic. At the international food festival, Sara tried Ethiopian injera, Peruvian ceviche, Korean kimchi, and Moroccan tagine, each more surprising than the last. Meanwhile, foreign visitors crowded around the Bangladeshi stall, photographing panta bhat and shutki as if they were rare treasures. Exotic means originating in a distant foreign country, or strikingly unusual. What feels exotic depends on where you stand. Think: external, from outside.

gre.s: The botanist travelled to remote islands in search of ____ plants that had never been described in any European catalogue.
gre.clue: had never been described in any European catalogue

example: Pet shops in Katabon sell exotic birds from Africa and South America, though some of them are smuggled into the country illegally.

en: To prevent something from succeeding; a person who contrasts with another
hook: FOIL: wrap the plan in FOIL so it can't work.
story: Foil. Three thieves planned to rob a mobile phone shop in Farmgate at midnight. But the night guard noticed their van circling the block, called the police, and switched on every light. The thieves fled empty-handed. The guard had foiled their plan: prevented it from succeeding. As a noun, a foil is a character who contrasts with another, making their qualities stand out. Steady, ordinary Watson is the perfect foil for brilliant Sherlock Holmes. Synonyms: thwart, frustrate, stymie.

gre.s: An alert bank clerk managed to ____ the robbery by quietly pressing a silent alarm, and the police arrived before the gang could reach the vault.
gre.clue: by quietly pressing a silent alarm

example: A sudden thunderstorm foiled the climbers' plan to reach the summit before noon, forcing them back to the lower camp.

en: The outer edge; unconventional or extreme views outside the mainstream
hook: FRINGE: the edge of a scarf, far from the center.
story: Fringe. Most economists at the conference agreed on the basic causes of inflation. But one speaker claimed that it was secretly caused by solar flares, and that the central bank should be run by astrologers. The audience politely ignored him. His views were fringe: far outside the mainstream. Literally, a fringe is the outer edge, like the threads on a shawl or the fringe of a forest. A fringe group sits at the edge of society or opinion. Synonyms: marginal, extreme, peripheral.

gre.s: Once dismissed as a ____ theory held by only a handful of eccentrics, the idea has since gained wide acceptance among mainstream scientists.
gre.clue: held by only a handful of eccentrics

example: The party began as a fringe movement meeting in a single tea shop, yet within a decade it had won seats in parliament.

en: Having a tendency or willingness to do something
hook: INCLINED: LEANING toward something, like an inclined plane.
story: Inclined. After a long day at the office, Arif's body leaned toward the sofa and the TV remote. He was inclined to skip the gym. Then his friend called: "I am outside. Let's go." He went anyway, and felt great afterward. Inclined means having a natural tendency or willingness to do something. "I am inclined to agree" means you lean toward agreement. Picture an inclined plane: everything tends to slide one way.

gre.s: Having been burned by investments before, she was not ____ to trust the salesman's promises of guaranteed returns.
gre.clue: Having been burned by investments before

example: After the long train ride, few of the tourists were inclined to climb the hundred steps up to the old temple.

en: Showing a lack of experience, wisdom, or judgment
hook: NAIVE: like a NATIVE newcomer who doesn't know the city's tricks.
story: Naive. On her first day in Dhaka, Ruma believed every rickshaw puller who said his fare was fixed, gave her phone number to a stranger promising a cheap flat, and paid for a genuine gold chain at a roadside stall. Her city cousins laughed. She was naive: showing a lack of experience, wisdom, or judgment. Naive comes from the same root as native, meaning born; a naive person is like a newborn in the world. Synonyms: credulous, gullible, ingenuous. Opposite: worldly.

gre.s: Only a ____ observer would take the company's promises at face value, since it has broken nearly every pledge it has made in the past decade.
gre.clue: since it has broken nearly every pledge it has made in the past decade

example: It was naive of the startup founders to assume that investors would fund them without first seeing any sales figures.

en: Not well known or hard to understand (adj.); to hide or make unclear (verb)
hook: OBSCURE: hidden in the dark (obscurity).
story: Obscure. In a dusty secondhand bookshop, Sara found a poem by an obscure village poet from the 1890s: nobody had heard of him, not even her literature professor. The poem's meaning was obscure too, full of strange references she could not decode. That night, clouds obscured the moon, hiding it completely. As an adjective, obscure means unknown or unclear. As a verb, it means to hide. The GRE uses both.

gre.s: Once an ____ figure known only to a few specialists, the painter is now celebrated in major museums around the world.
gre.clue: known only to a few specialists

example: The prizewinning novel first appeared from an obscure press in Rajshahi that had never sold more than a few hundred copies of any title.

en: Very great or intense; having deep insight
hook: PROFOUND: as deep as the ocean FOUNDATION.
story: Profound. When Anika's grandfather was dying, he called her to his bed and said only one sentence: 'Spend your life on people, not on things.' She has never forgotten it. Those few words had a profound effect on her: very great and intense. A profound remark is one with deep insight. Pro means forward and fund means bottom: profound reaches toward the bottom, deep. Its opposite is superficial or shallow. Synonyms: deep, intense, insightful.

gre.s: Although the lecture was delivered in simple language, its insights were ____, forcing listeners to reconsider assumptions they had held all their lives.
gre.clue: forcing listeners to reconsider assumptions they had held all their lives

example: The simple question of why the night sky is dark turned out to have profound implications for our picture of the universe.

en: To cause to become; to provide or give
hook: RENDER: RENDERS it into a new state.
story: Render. The night before her thesis was due, a power surge fried Moushumi's laptop and rendered it useless. Her friend Tanha arrived at midnight with her own computer and rendered all the help she could, retyping chapters until dawn. To render is to cause to become, as in rendered useless or rendered speechless. It also means to provide or give: to render a service, to render aid. A court renders a verdict, and a singer renders a song. Synonyms: make, provide, deliver.

gre.s: Throughout the crisis, volunteers continued to ____ assistance to stranded travelers, offering food, shelter, and free rides to the nearest town.
gre.clue: offering food, shelter, and free rides to the nearest town

example: Local fishermen rendered vital help to the coast guard, guiding rescue boats through channels that did not appear on any chart.

en: Shy and quiet, preferring to stay out of sight
hook: GRE trick: RETIRING means shy — she RETIRES to her room when guests come.
story: Retiring. At every family gathering, Priya's cousin Sabbir sits quietly in a corner with a book. He smiles when spoken to but never starts a conversation, and he slips away before the group photographs. He is retiring: shy and tending to avoid company. This has nothing to do with stopping work at sixty, though both involve withdrawing. A retiring person withdraws from attention. Synonyms: reserved, diffident, shy.

gre.s: Though her paintings were bold and flamboyant, the artist herself was ____, avoiding interviews and rarely appearing even at her own exhibitions.
gre.clue: avoiding interviews and rarely appearing even at her own exhibitions

example: The retiring mathematician declined every invitation to speak about her famous proof and went on quietly teaching first-year calculus.

en: The art of persuasive speaking or writing; sometimes, language that is impressive but insincere
hook: RHETORIC: a RHETORICAL question doesn't need an answer — it's just for effect.
story: Rhetoric. Before the student union election, two candidates spoke. The first promised 'a golden new dawn' and 'a campus reborn', without one concrete plan. The second quietly listed three repairs she would make to the library. The crowd cheered the first, but Arif called it empty rhetoric: impressive but insincere language. Rhetoric is also the respectable art of persuasive speaking and writing, studied since ancient Greece. A rhetorical question expects no answer. Synonyms: oratory, bombast, grandiloquence.

gre.s: Voters had grown weary of the candidate's ____, noting that years of grand speeches had produced not a single new road or school.
gre.clue: years of grand speeches had produced not a single new road or school

example: Behind the minister's rhetoric about a digital revolution, most village schools still had no computers and no reliable electricity.

en: Strong, sturdy, and healthy; vigorous
hook: ROBUST: like a ROBOT, strong and hard to break.
story: Robust. Farhan's father still uses an old Nokia phone from 2006. It has fallen off the roof, been run over by a bicycle, and spent a whole night in a monsoon puddle. Every time, it switched on and rang. The family calls it the brick. It is robust: strong, sturdy, and hard to break. Robust health, a robust economy, robust evidence: all of them can withstand pressure. Think of a robot built to last.

gre.s: Far from being fragile, the economy proved surprisingly ____, recovering within months from a shock that analysts had expected to last years.
gre.clue: Far from being fragile

example: Bamboo scaffolding is surprisingly robust, and Dhaka builders still use it to put up apartment towers many storeys high.

en: To go around the edge of; to avoid dealing with an issue
hook: GRE trick: to SKIRT means to go around the edge, like a skirt's hem.
story: Skirt. The highway into town was flooded, so the bus skirted the town centre, taking the outer road around its edge. That evening, a journalist asked the mayor about the flooded roads. The mayor talked about new parks, cricket results, and tourism, but never once about the flooding. He skirted the question. To skirt is to go around the edge of something, or to avoid dealing with a difficult topic. Picture walking along the hem of a skirt.

gre.s: Rather than addressing the scandal directly, the spokesperson tried to ____ the issue by talking at length about the company's charitable work.
gre.clue: Rather than addressing the scandal directly

example: The new history textbook skirts the controversy over the war's causes, offering a list of dates instead of an explanation.

en: Serious and sensible; not drunk
hook: GRE trick: SOBER means serious and realistic, not just alcohol-free.
story: Sober. At a wedding in Sylhet, the music was loud and the guests were joyful. But when news came that the bride's grandfather had collapsed, the mood turned sober at once: serious and sensible. Guests lowered their voices and the band stopped playing. Sober also means not drunk, and on the GRE it often describes calm, realistic judgment, as in a sober assessment. A sober suit is plain, not flashy. Synonyms: serious, solemn, restrained, levelheaded.

gre.s: After years of wildly optimistic forecasts, the committee's latest report offered a more ____ assessment, acknowledging that the economy might not recover for a decade.
gre.clue: acknowledging that the economy might not recover for a decade

example: A sober look at the club's finances showed that it could not afford a foreign coach for at least two more seasons.

en: Serious, strict, and unyielding
hook: STERN: like the STERN (back) of a ship, firm and unmoving.
story: Stern. When the principal walked into the assembly hall, eight hundred students stopped talking instantly. She did not smile. She did not raise her voice. She simply stood at the front, hands folded, and looked at the latecomers. Every one of them felt that look. Her face was stern: serious, strict, and unyielding. A stern warning means you had better listen. Think of the stern of a ship: firm, solid, and not moving.

gre.s: Behind the judge's ____ exterior, which intimidated many lawyers, lay a deeply compassionate person.
gre.clue: which intimidated many lawyers

example: The referee gave the captain a stern warning, and for the rest of the match nobody dared to argue with a single decision.

en: Shaped by one's own feelings and tastes, not by facts
hook: SUBJECTIVE: depends on the SUBJECT, the person judging.
story: Subjective. Is kacchi biryani better than tehari? Rafi says yes, absolutely, no contest. Mitu says no, never, tehari wins forever. They argued for an hour and neither was wrong, because taste is subjective: based on personal feelings and preferences, not measurable facts. Subjective is the opposite of objective. A judge should be objective; a food critic can be subjective. Think: it depends on the subject, the person doing the judging.

gre.s: Because judges' scores in the competition are inevitably ____, organizers introduced a panel of five to reduce the influence of any one person's taste.
gre.clue: reduce the influence of any one person's taste

example: Pain is partly subjective, so two patients with the same injury may describe it in very different ways.

en: To make something milder or less extreme
hook: GRE trick: to TEMPER is to TONE DOWN, like tempering spicy food with yogurt.
story: Temper. Priya wrote a furious online review of a restaurant that had served her cold biryani. Before posting it, she read it again and decided it was too harsh. She removed the insults, mentioned the friendly waiter, and tempered her criticism: she moderated and softened it. As a verb, to temper is to moderate. Blacksmiths temper steel, heating and cooling it so it is less brittle. Losing your temper is the opposite of tempering anything. Synonyms: moderate, soften, mitigate.

gre.s: Hoping to ____ the committee's harsh conclusions, the chair added a paragraph acknowledging the team's genuine achievements under difficult conditions.
gre.clue: acknowledging the team's genuine achievements

example: Grandfather tempered his strict rules with generous helpings of sweets, so the children never stayed angry with him for long.

en: Complete with regard to every detail
hook: THOROUGH: goes THROUGH everything.
story: Thorough. Before submitting her university application, Mitu printed everything and checked it line by line: every document, every date, every spelling, every signature. It took a whole day. She found two small mistakes, a wrong year and a misspelled professor's name, that could have cost her admission. Her check was thorough: complete with regard to every detail. Its opposite is cursory. Think: it goes through everything.

gre.s: Unlike the hasty earlier investigation, the new inquiry was ____, interviewing every witness and examining every document.
gre.clue: interviewing every witness and examining every document

example: Before buying the secondhand car, Imtiaz asked a mechanic to do a thorough check of the brakes, engine, and wiring.

en: Done for appearance only; a symbol or sign
hook: TOKEN: just a symbolic gesture, like a TOKEN coin.
story: Token. After complaints that its board had no women, a company appointed a single woman director, but gave her no vote on major decisions and left her out of key meetings. Critics called it a token gesture: done for appearance only. Joya's grandmother used the word differently when she gave Joya a silver bangle as a token of her love: a symbol or sign. A token payment is a small, symbolic one. Synonyms: nominal, symbolic, perfunctory.

gre.s: The government's ____ efforts at reform, which changed a few official titles but left the corrupt system entirely untouched, fooled no one.
gre.clue: changed a few official titles but left the corrupt system entirely untouched

example: The landlord made a token repair, painting over the damp patch on the wall without fixing the leaking pipe behind it.

en: Never done or known before
hook: UN-PRECEDENT-ED: no PRECEDENT, never happened before.
story: Unprecedented. In 2022, floodwater in parts of Sylhet rose higher than anyone could remember. Elders who had lived through decades of monsoons said they had never seen anything like it. Newspapers called the flood unprecedented: never done or known before. A precedent is an earlier example that guides later decisions, so unprecedented means having no earlier example at all. Lawyers search for precedents; an unprecedented case has none. Synonyms: unparalleled, unheard of, novel.

gre.s: The flood was truly ____: in two hundred years of written records, the river had never risen even half as high.
gre.clue: had never risen even half as high

example: The team's run of fourteen straight victories was unprecedented in the league's sixty-year history.

en: Practical and able to succeed; workable
hook: VIABLE: has VITALITY, can survive.
story: Viable. Sakib wanted to open a rooftop café in Dhanmondi. Before investing his savings, he studied the rent, counted the people passing by each evening, priced the coffee, and estimated how many customers he needed each day. The numbers worked. The plan was viable: capable of working successfully, feasible. Viable comes from French vie, life; a viable seed can live and grow. Synonyms: feasible, workable, practicable. Opposite: unworkable.

gre.s: Although solar power was once dismissed as too expensive, falling costs have made it a ____ alternative to coal in many countries.
gre.clue: falling costs have made it

example: Floating schools built on boats have proved a viable option for children in villages that monsoon floods cut off for months.
